01 — Federated learningCase studyCh. 01 / 08

01 — Problem

Facial-image datasets for ASD research are small, scattered across institutions and too sensitive to pool.

Federated learning trains one model without moving the images: in the study design, each site trains locally and shares only model weights. That changes what has to travel, but not what the model can claim. ASD diagnosis is clinical and behavioural, so a classifier like this is a research instrument, never a diagnosis.

Privacy
Raw images stay on each site; only weights and sample counts travel.
Data
Small datasets held by different institutions.
Compute
A frozen backbone, so each round trains only a small head.
Ethics
Research only: every prediction carries a disclaimer, and no faces appear on this site.

“Not a diagnostic tool.”

The dashboard shows a research disclaimer with every prediction

03 — Federated learningCase studyCh. 03 / 08

03 — Technical architecture

Two halves with different standards of proof: a training design the team describes, and an inference path anyone can read.

Fig. 3.3 · Federated study design, full

Scroll sideways to follow the whole drawing.
  1. 1Clients. Three data silos; images stay on site. As described; code not public.
  2. 2Local model. Frozen EfficientNetB0, global average pooling, dense 256 and 128 with dropout, one sigmoid output; Adam at 1e-4 with binary cross-entropy. Verified from the checkpoint.
  3. 3Server. Flower with federated averaging: each client’s weights count in proportion to its sample count. As described; code not public.
  4. 4Best checkpoint. A Keras .h5 file in the public repository.
  5. 5Streamlit dashboard. Runs locally: upload, resize to 224 pixels, predict.
  6. 6Output. A label and a score capped at 99%, with a research-only disclaimer.
04 — Federated learningCase studyCh. 04 / 08

04 — Key challenges and decisions

  1. D1

    Freeze the backbone.

    Only a head of about 361,000 parameters is trained, so each round’s update is small. The size is verified from the checkpoint’s config; the motivation is inferred.

  2. D2

    Average by sample count.

    Federated averaging weights each client by how many samples it trained on, so a large silo counts for more than a small one. The lab on this page lets you change the counts.

  3. D3

    Say what it is not.

    The dashboard shows a research disclaimer with every prediction, and the score is capped at 99%.

Weight the client updates.

Each client trains locally and sends one parameter w. The server weights each update by that client’s share of the samples, n ÷ N, and adds them up.

With every count at 0 there is nothing to weight: N = 0, and the average is undefined.

Open on the home bench
Follow one training round

Local training

Each client trains a copy of the model using its own images. The raw images stay with that client.

Model updates

The three clients send the parameters learned from their local datasets to the coordinator.

Aggregation

The coordinator averages the updates and shares the resulting model with the clients for their next training round.

07 — Federated learningCase studyCh. 07 / 08

07 — Evaluation, results and limitations

Results will be added with the published paper.

Limitations

  • This is not a diagnostic tool. ASD diagnosis is clinical and behavioural.
  • Public ASD face datasets are web-scraped, with unverified labels, so accuracy may reflect dataset artefacts.
  • Per-population results are not public.
  • Federated learning alone does not guarantee privacy: no secure aggregation or differential privacy is evidenced.
  • The training and federation code is not public, so the dashed half of Fig. 3.3 cannot be checked yet.
